title: Income timing, family support, and budget margin distribute unevenly across US households
source_unit: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking adult respondent and family, 2025

observations.period: 2025 SHED; income sources and public assistance

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; publication percentages use the all-adult respondent frame

labor_income.unit: percent of adults and spouse/partner receiving wages, salaries, or self-employment income in prior year

government_housing_assistance.unit: percent of adults reporting family receipt in prior 12 months

government_food_assistance.unit: percent of adults reporting family receipt in prior 12 months

outside_household_expense_help.unit: percent of adults receiving help with a listed expense in prior 12 months

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published tables; respondents could select multiple income sources and assistance types, and labor income includes spouse/partner income.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported receipt and source measures do not establish adequacy, eligibility, transfer size, timing, or whether help prevented hardship; question universes differ across tables.
observations.subgroup: All adults, with age-conditioned assistance and outside-help estimates reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Multiple income sources or assistance can provide resilience, but can also signal dependence or a need that is not captured by aggregate income.

observations.period: 2023 to 2025 SHED; monthly income variability and hardship

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; income-variability questions use the applicable adult respondent frame

employee_income_variability.unit: percent of adults working for someone else in month before survey

observations.method: Repeated SHED descriptive comparison of self-reported month-to-month income variation and bill difficulty attributed by respondents to that variation.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is not a panel result, and the attribution to income variation is respondent-reported; employment selection, income level, benefits, and schedule differences may confound subgroup gaps.
observations.subgroup: All adults, self-employed adults, employees, retirees, and non-retirees.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income variability may be manageable when households have savings, credit, benefits, or flexible timing; variability is not identical to insecurity.

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; all-adult respondent frame

monthly_income_increased.unit: percent of adults versus 12 months earlier

monthly_spending_increased.unit: percent of adults versus 12 months earlier

money_left_over_under_25k.unit: percent of adults with family income under $25,000

money_left_over_100k_plus.unit: percent of adults with family income of $100,000 or more

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED published descriptive estimates; increases in monthly income and spending are separate reports, and the money-left-over measure is a separate budget-margin question.
observations.uncertainty: Annual self-reports do not measure account balances, exact spending categories, debt service, or the timing mismatch between income and expenses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher spending can reflect improved consumption or necessary price increases; a month-end surplus can be temporary and does not establish durable financial security.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; price response and anticipatory consumption

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; action questions allow multiple responses

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published action estimates; selected actions are not mutually exclusive and are self-reported responses over the prior 12 months.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not identify which price caused an action, whether a response was protective or deprivation, or whether it persisted after prices changed.
observations.subgroup: All adults; anticipatory purchase measure has separate family-income comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Switching, delaying, or buying early can be strategic consumption; reduced saving, borrowing, or extra work can reflect either chosen smoothing or constrained room.

related_sources.claim: Overall SHED 2025 financial-well-being context and methodology.

boundary: This record establishes Federal Reserve 2025 SHED distributions for income sources, outside support, income variability, budget margin, and price adaptations. It does not establish a dated shock-to-response causal path, benefit adequacy, household recovery, trust, political action, or cultural meaning.
